Pre-eclampsia affects 5–8% of pregnancies and is a leading cause of maternal and infant mortality if not identified early. Regular blood pressure monitoring at every antenatal visit is essential.

Breast Health Awareness: Know Your Body, Protect Your Future
Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among women in India, accounting for approximately 14% of all female cancer diagnoses. While these statistics are sobering, the message behind them is hopeful: when detected early, breast cancer has an excellent prognosis, with survival rates exceeding 90% at Stage 1.

The challenge is that early breast cancer often presents with no symptoms at all — which is precisely why awareness, self-examination, and routine screening are so critical.

Breast self-examination (BSE): Every woman above the age of 20 should perform a monthly breast self-check, ideally a week after her period ends. Familiarity with your own breast tissue helps you detect changes early.

What to look for:
• A new lump or thickening in the breast or armpit
• Changes in the size, shape, or contour of the breast
• Skin dimpling, puckering, or redness
• Nipple inversion (turning inward) or unusual nipple discharge
• Persistent breast pain not related to your menstrual cycle

Clinical breast examination: All women should have a clinical breast examination by their gynaecologist annually from age 25 or 30.

Mammography: Recommended annually or biennially from age 40 — or earlier for women with a family history of breast cancer.

Women with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer may benefit from genetic counselling and BRCA1/BRCA2 testing.

Contraception: Choosing the Right Option for Your Life Stage
Family planning is one of the most empowering aspects of women's healthcare—yet many women continue to rely on methods that may not be the best fit for their health, lifestyle, or future plans. With a wide range of safe, effective contraceptive options now available, every woman deserves a personalised conversation about what is right for her.

Common contraceptive options and who they suit:

Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (COCP): Highly effective, regulates periods, reduces cramps and acne. Suitable for most healthy women. Requires daily consistency. Not recommended for those with certain clotting disorders or migraines.

Progestogen-Only Pill (Mini Pill): Suitable for breastfeeding mothers, women who cannot take oestrogen, or those over 35 who smoke.

Intrauterine Device (IUD / Copper Coil): Non-hormonal, long-acting (up to 10 years), highly effective. Good for women seeking hormone-free contraception.

Hormonal IUS (Mirena): Reduces or eliminates periods, excellent for women with heavy or painful periods. Effective for 5 years.

Injectable Contraception (DMPA): Once every 3 months. Suitable for women who prefer not to think about daily or weekly methods.

Implant (Nexplanon): A small rod placed under the skin of the upper arm — effective for 3 years with over 99% efficacy.

Emergency Contraception: Available for use within 72–120 hours of unprotected intercourse. Not intended for regular use.

Understanding Fibroids: What Every Woman Should Know
Uterine fibroids are non-cancerous growths of the uterus that appear during the reproductive years. They are extraordinarily common — studies suggest up to 70–80% of women will develop fibroids by age 50 — yet many women know very little about them until symptoms become severe.

Fibroids vary widely in size (from a pea to the size of a melon), number, and location within or on the uterus. Their location largely determines whether they cause symptoms.

Types of uterine fibroids:
• Submucosal — grow inside the uterine cavity; most likely to cause heavy bleeding and fertility issues
• Intramural — grow within the uterine wall; most common type
• Subserosal — grow on the outer surface of the uterus; may press on surrounding organs
• Pedunculated — attached to the uterus by a stalk; can twist and cause acute pain

Common symptoms include heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, pelvic pressure or pain, frequent urination, constipation, backache, and in some cases, difficulty conceiving or complications during pregnancy.

Importantly, many fibroids cause no symptoms at all and are discovered incidentally during routine ultrasound.
